01Bases & the finished rim

Intro lecture · slides 2–11

Base characteristics

  • Strength and rigidity: a wax base must incorporate a strengthener
  • Accuracy: the base must not rock on the master cast
  • Smooth, rounded, well-polished borders
  • Thickness of borders and palate resembles the finished denture
    • Palate 1–2 mm (depends on base material)
    • Border thickness/contour defined by the land area; base must not extend onto the land area
    • Post dam area chamfers into the palate
    • Dentate case: wax chamfers into the teeth

Base materials

  • Wax base: modelling wax, requires a strengthener (wire, light cure, metal)
  • Acrylic base: heat cure, cold cure
  • Others: light cure resin, tray resin, thermoformed, shellac

Block out undercuts and frenums, rugae, irregular surfaces and redundant tissue areas, then separator so it doesn't adhere: listed for cold cure acrylic and vacuum-formed bases. Shellac also needs block-out.

Base materials compared

MaterialHow it's made (slide steps)ProsCons
Acrylic: cold cureBlock out → separator → salt & pepper technique → finished (clear or pink)Very accurate · good for finding high spots · good for precision workVery expensive · time consuming
Acrylic: heat cureWax base ready for processing → processed base trimmed & polished → base with occlusal rimsVery accurate · finding high spots · precision workVery expensive · time consuming
Light cure resinMaterial → model prep → light cure adaptation → trimmed extensions → curing basesStable · inexpensiveBrittle · will require wash impression
Tray resinLiquid & powder → mix → final mix → wait for dough stage → flatten → adapt to modelInexpensive · rigidMessy & time sensitive · non-uniform thickness · possible chemical sensitivity
ThermoformedThermoform blank → base (clear or coloured) on a pressure or vacuum thermoforming unit. Vacuum formed = vinyl and polyethyleneCan be clear · accurateEquipment expensive · flexible
ShellacShellac blank → adapted by heat (malleable, moulded over model) → finishedThin · inexpensiveHeat sensitive · susceptible to distortion · time sensitive
Wax + strengthenerWire, light cure or preformed alloy strengthenerInexpensive · quick to produce · easy to adjustNot as stable as a rigid base · wax can distort unless a preformed alloy strengthener is used (increases cost)

Strengtheners

Finished product should…

This exact checklist is on the Intro, Edentulous and Partials decks. Grouped here so it's easier to recall.

Build quality

  • Be stable and rigid
  • Have good adaptation
  • Have correct dimensions
  • Wax smooth and free of voids
  • Constructed on the secondary model

Thickness & extensions

  • Palate no more than 2 mm thick
  • Do not cover land area
  • Extensions not past the post dam
  • Frenums relieved
  • Smooth and rounded borders
  • Incorporate buccal roll in all cases

Rim position & shape

  • Rim centred over the crest of the ridge
  • Anterior curvature simulates the curvature of the arch
  • Upper posterior section tapered to avoid the retromolar pad
  • Partials: height and width same as natural dentition

Soft tissue space

  • Space allowed for tongue and cheeks
  • Lingual contours must not impinge on tongue space
  • Contour for posterior cheek space

02Clinical records

Intro lecture · slides 12–22

A registration rim records…

…the information required to produce a trial denture.

Jaw relationship records, transferred to the articulator by an MMR record using the master models:

  • Vertical dimension
  • Centric relation
  • Occlusal plane
  • Neutral zone

Also used to record:

  • Labial contour
  • Midline
  • Intercanine distance
  • Smile line
  • Aids in tooth selection
RuleALL records required must be taken prior to using the facebow.

Grooves cut in the rims

  • Upper: for location on the bite fork
  • Lower: for location on the MMR bite record

Records slide list

Vertical dimension · Free-way space · Centric relation · Occlusal plane · Labial contour · Midline · Intercanine distance · Smile line · Aids in tooth selection

What each record tells you

Labial contour

Rim contoured until the desired lip and cheek contours are obtained. A properly contoured anterior rim aids in positioning the anterior teeth.

Occlusal plane

Rim used with a Fox occlusal plane to verify level and angulation; adjusted to the landmarks; once articulated, lets teeth be set at the correct level. Incisal edge of the central incisor matches the occlusal height.

Vertical dimension

Rims are an aid to determine the proper vertical dimension of occlusion, make centric relation records and transfer them to the articulator for setting up artificial teeth.

Speech

Thick maxillary record bases and convex mandibular contours impinge on tongue space, so the patient can't articulate speech sounds normally. Wax base no thicker than 2 mm.

Midline

Where the centrals will be positioned.

Intercanine distance

The width of the teeth to be selected.

Smile line

The length of the teeth to be selected.

Shape of rim

Matches the shape of the patient's arch and face; teeth are selected using this shape, or from existing dentures.

Partials

Same records list for partial acrylic and partial frameworks. The rim always depends on the position of the natural teeth.

03Edentulous rims

Edentulous lecture · slides 2–9

Model prep: mark…

  1. Crest of ridge posteriorly
  2. Anterior crest of ridge
  3. Land area, so you can locate the crest of the ridge

Wax base

upperlower where the two differ
  1. Follow SWPs
  2. Ensure the model is wet
  3. Mark crest of ridge
  4. Soften wax evenly
  5. Ensure wax is well adapted
  6. Ensure wax goes to full extensions
  7. Ensure wax is rolled for smooth peripheries
  8. Do not cover the land area
  9. Incorporate a strengthener
    appropriate strengthener: must not interfere with or thicken the post-dam areawire strengthener, minimum length from 16 to 26 area
  10. Ensure a second layer of wax is added
  11. Ensure there is a uniform thickness of wax

Wax rim

  1. Follow SWPs
  2. Measure length of wax
    maxillary tuberosity → tuberositymandibular retromolar pad → retromolar pad
  3. Heat wax uniformly
  4. Roll wax to create a solid tube
  5. Place rim directly over the crest of ridge
  6. Seal rim to base (buccally and lingually)
  7. Correct height by flattening on bench with wax paper
    anterior and tuberosity heightanterior and retromolar pad height
  8. Trim maxillary to allow room for the retromolar pad
    upper only
  9. Wax in concave areas, buccal and lingual, with molten wax
  10. Mark line over crest of ridge
  11. Trim rim to correct width anteriorly and posteriorly

Finishing

  1. Follow SWPs
  2. Use the correct flame
  3. Move brush flame constantly
  4. Fill any holes with hot wax knife
  5. Remove all flash buccally and lingually
  6. Brush flame periphery areas again on the model (not buccal roll)
  7. Polish wax with a cotton wool bud in cold soapy water
  8. Wash all the soap off in clean water
  9. Keep rims on models to avoid distortion

04Partial acrylic rims

Partials lecture · slides 2–8

Slide labelSlides 2 and 3 are both titled "Wax bases – Upper". Slide 3's content and photos are the lower (lingual trim, tongue space, wire strengthener, 2/3–1/3 rule), so it's shown as lower here.

Wax base

upperlower where the two differ
  1. Follow SWPs
  2. Ensure the model is wet
  3. Soften wax evenly
  4. Measure wax allowing for sulcus depth
  5. Ensure wax is well adapted
  6. Ensure wax goes to full extensions
  7. Cut wax to marginal ridge height (posteriors)
  8. Cut wax over the anteriors
    just above cervical margin over the cingulums (if bite allows)2/3 above cervical margin, 1/3 below incisal edge
  9. Cut along mesial or distal of abutting teeth
  10. Trim to sulcus depth
    buccallybuccally and lingually, keeping tongue space clear
  11. Ease frenums
  12. Chamfer the wax into the teeth so there is no step at the finishing point
  13. Strengthener
    appropriate strengthener, must not interfere with or thicken post-damwire strengthener, minimum length from 16 to 26 area
  14. Add a second layer of wax
  15. Trim to the same extensions as the first layer
  16. Ensure uniform thickness of wax
  17. Brush flame and smooth
  18. Check the occlusion

Wax rim

  1. Follow SWPs
  2. Measure length of wax to match space
  3. Heat wax uniformly
  4. Roll wax to create a solid tube
  5. Place rim directly over the crest of ridge
  6. Seal rim to base buccally and lingually using a hot wax knife
  7. Height to match natural teeth by flattening on bench with wax paper
  8. Do not push too hard or you will break your teeth
  9. Wax in concave areas, buccal and lingual, with molten wax using hot wax knife
  10. Trim maxillary to allow room for the retromolar pad
    upper only
  11. Mark width of natural teeth and trim to that width (anteriorly and posteriorly)
  12. Re-trim wax if necessary
    • Around posterior natural teeth to marginal ridge height
    • Along mesial or distal of abutting teeth
    • Anteriors:
    just above cervical margin over cingulums (if bite allows)2/3 above cervical margin, 1/3 below incisal edge

Finishing (upper and lower identical)

  1. Follow SWPs
  2. Use the correct flame
  3. Move brush flame constantly
  4. Fill any holes with hot wax knife
  5. Remove all flash buccally and lingually
  6. Relieve any frenums
  7. Smooth peripheries with hot wax knife
  8. Smooth wax around natural teeth, do not shorten
  9. Smooth wax along post dam, do not touch tissue fitting surface
  10. Brush flame periphery areas again on the model (not buccal roll)
  11. Polish with a cotton wool bud in cold soapy water
  12. Wash all the soap off in clean water
  13. Keep rims on models to avoid distortion

05Articulation

Articulation 2026 · slides 2–17

Definitions

Dental articulation is the dynamic contact relationship between the upper (maxillary) and lower (mandibular) teeth during jaw movements such as chewing, speaking or swallowing. It covers static tooth alignment (occlusion) and the sliding motions of the jaw (protrusion and lateral excursions).

An articulator is a mechanical device that mimics the TMJ and jaw movements.

The correct relationship is transferred by an MMR record to the articulator using the master models, using maxillary and mandibular registration rims or a squash bite.

Articulator types

Simple

  1. Disposable (crown & bridge)
  2. Plasterless (mouthguards)
  3. Plasterless with mounted models
  4. Plain line (hinge movement only)
  5. Plain line with mounted models

Semi-adjustable

  1. Denar: previous, most expensive
  2. Hanau: current, medium cost
  3. Alanden: medium cost
  4. Treedental: cheapest

Fully adjustable

Differs from semi-adjustable by the addition of more condylar movements.

Hanau Wide-Vue articulator

Components

  • Mounting plates
  • Incisal pin
  • Incisal guide (table)
  • Condylar guidance
Average setting (zeroing)Value
Incisal pin0° dark mark
pin end matches middle mark
Incisal table: protrusive0 = 30°
Incisal table: lateral0°
will change with teeth
Condyles: Bennett angle15°
Condyles: condylar track30°
Don't mix upThe manufacturer diagram labels "30° Bennett angles", but the average setting taught is Bennett angle 15° and condylar track 30°.

Springbow

Other terms

Earbow · Facebow

Components

  • Springbow
  • Ear-pieces (×2)
  • Reference pointer
  • Bite fork
  • Anterior elevating assembly
  • Transfer clamp assembly
  • Mounting platform with cast support

Mounting the maxillary model

Before plaster (edentulous)

  1. Check incisal pin, incisal table and condyles are set correctly
  2. Cut relocation grooves in upper model base
  3. Ensure model is wet for proper bonding
  4. Connect mounting platform, with cast support, to articulator
  5. Ensure there is enough space between the plate and model

Plaster: Place, Place, Support, Ensure, Carve, Smooth, Finish

  1. Place plaster in retention grooves of articulator plate
  2. Place plaster on upper model and close articulator
  3. Support facebow so it does not distort
  4. Ensure the incisal pin contacts the incisal table
  5. Carve plaster to land area and plate around whole of the model
  6. Smooth plaster with water and fingers
  7. Finish with sandpaper when plaster is firm

Mounting the mandibular model

  1. Ensure lower model locates with upper using a correct MMR and secure so it does not move
  2. Ensure model is wet for proper bonding
  3. Place plaster in retention grooves of articulator plate
  4. Place plaster on lower model
  5. Close articulator ensuring incisal pin contacts
  6. Carve plaster to land area and plate around whole of the model
  7. Smooth plaster with water and fingers
  8. When plaster is firm, finish with sandpaper

Dentate vs edentulous mounting

EdentulousDentate
MaxillaryPrep steps, then plaster; "Support facebow so it does not distort"Same plaster steps; "Ensure facebow is supported by the mounting platform, with cast support"
MandibularIdentical steps for both: locate with correct MMR and secure → wet → plaster in plate grooves → plaster on model → close, incisal pin contacts → carve → smooth → sandpaper
